content: 1. Chronic manifestations of lymphatic filariasis (LF) include acute attacks, lymphedema (commonly referred to as elephantiasis), and hydrocele. 2. Acute attacks are characterized by the sudden onset of limb swelling, redness, warmth, and pain, which may or may not be accompanied by fever, chills, headache, and weakness. Management involves antibiotic therapy targeting common skin bacteria such as Streptococcus and Staphylococcus species. Symptomatic management includes the use of analgesics, anti-inflammatory medications, antipyretics, and supportive measures such as rest, limb elevation, hydration, and cooling of the affected area. Hygiene should be maintained as tolerated. Harmful practices, such as popping blisters or damaging the skin, should be avoided. Antifilarial medications like diethylcarbamazine (DEC) are not recommended during acute attacks. 3. Lymphedema management focuses on hygiene, skin and wound care, limb elevation, regular low-intensity exercises, and wearing comfortable shoes. The affected area should be washed daily with soap and clean water, dried carefully, and protected from injury. Small wounds should be treated with antiseptics or antibiotic creams, and antifungal creams can prevent fungal infections in deep skin folds. Elevation of the affected limb promotes lymphatic flow, and exercises help maintain joint mobility and lymphatic drainage. 4. Hydrocele, a condition involving progressive scrotal swelling, is generally painless and not associated with redness. Surgical intervention, specifically hydrocelectomy, is the definitive treatment. Surgery improves scrotal size, patient quality of life, and functionality. Preoperative and postoperative care, including physical exams and ultrasound, is essential to ensure successful outcomes. 5. Hygiene kits for lymphedema management may include unscented soap, clean towels or gauze, antibacterial and antifungal creams, antiseptics, and patient education materials. These measures can often be performed at home by the patient or with family assistance. Community health workers can support patients in maintaining these practices and refer them for further care when necessary. 6. Adjunct measures for lymphedema, such as compressive bandaging and lymphatic massage, may not be feasible in resource-limited settings but can be considered in comprehensive health systems with skilled staff. 7. Hydrocelectomy is recommended for all stages of hydrocele to prevent progression to more severe stages. The surgical technique, often involving excision with electrocautery, should be performed by experienced surgeons in properly equipped operating rooms. Preoperative antibiotics and appropriate skin preparation are critical to reducing surgical site infections. Postoperative care includes observation for at least 72 hours and dressing changes to minimize infection risks. 8. Antifilarial medications should be provided to individuals with positive filarial test strip (FTS) results or evidence of microfilaremia to eliminate microfilariae. However, patients with lymphedema or hydrocele who test negative for filarial antigen or microfilariae do not require antifilarial treatment. 9. Limited evidence suggests that a 4-6 week course of doxycycline (200 mg per day) may stabilize or reverse disease progression in lymphedema patients. Ongoing clinical trials are evaluating its effectiveness, and WHO will update recommendations based on emerging evidence. 10. Strategic planning for LF management aligns with the Sustainable Development Goals and aims to provide care for all individuals with disease manifestations. This includes strengthening local surgical capacity and ensuring access to essential care in endemic countries.
